whatIsThis.heading: What is this?
whatIsThis.body1: AutomataLab is an interactive workshop for
whatIsThis.subject: Formal Languages and Automata Theory
whatIsThis.body2: : finite automata, pushdown automata, Turing machines and generative grammars can be defined, simulated and transformed. Everything works offline, worksheets are saved to the browser automatically.

machines.heading: Machines — a single model
machines.body1: Every machine is built with the same
machines.body2: key: a finite control plus any number of storages.
machines.emphasis: Its kind is decided by the configuration
machines.body3: — no storage means a finite automaton, one stack means a pushdown automaton, tapes only (the input on one of them) mean a Turing machine — with several, a k-tape one —, another combination means a general machine. The interface recognizes it and names it accordingly.
machines.example:
Machine:               # finite automaton: no storage
  name: M_1
  charset: a, b
  states: S, A, F
  init: S
  accept: F
  transitions:         # δ(q, a) = p is written (q, a) -> p
    - (S, a) -> S
    - (S, b) -> S
    - (S, a) -> A
    - (A, b) -> F      # an ε-transition: (S, ε) -> A (type eps)

names.heading: Names
names.body: A name is a single letter with an optional subscript: M, M₁, X_a, M_{even}. Type _ to start a subscript and → to leave it; digits typed right after the letter go into the subscript by themselves (M1 becomes M₁). So AB in an expression is A followed by B. Function names (det, min, toRegex, …) are words, as sin is in mathematics. State names are free labels (AB, 00, {A,B}).

expressions.heading: Expressions
expressions.body1: In a new cell you can reference machines and perform operations in the form
expressions.body2: . If an operation's precondition is missing (e.g. ε-freedom for determinization), the app explains why and inserts the fix chain with one click.

storages.heading: Storages: stack, queue, tape
storages.example:
Machine:               # pushdown automaton: one stack
  name: P
  charset: a, b
  states: q0, q1, q2
  init: q0
  accept: q2           # or acceptMode: emptyStorages
  storages:
    stack: stack       # starts with Z; its alphabet is the symbols it uses
  transitions:         #   or: stack: { type: stack, charset: [Z, A], init: Z }
    - (q0, a, Z) -> (q0, AZ)   # reading a with Z on top: AZ instead of Z
    - (q0, b, A) -> (q1, ε)    # ε = push nothing
    - (q1, ε, Z) -> (q2, Z)    # ε-step (type eps)

Machine:               # Turing machine: one tape, holding the input
  name: T
  charset: a, b
  states: s, ok
  init: s
  accept: ok
  input: tape          # the input is placed on this storage
  storages:
    tape:
      type: tape
      charset: a, b, x, _   # Γ: Σ, the blank _ and more (by default Σ and _)
  transitions:
    - (s, a) -> (s, x, R)    # read a, write x, move right (R, L, S: right, left, stay)
    - (s, _) -> (ok, _, S)   # _ = the blank
storages.body1: A transition is written as δ in the lecture notes:
storages.body2: — δ's arguments are the state, the symbol read and what each storage reads (a stack's top, a tape's cell); its value is the next state and what each storage gets (the word pushed; the symbol written and the move). A tape is infinite to the right from its first cell, as in the lecture notes: a head stepping left off it halts the machine with an error (infinite: both makes it infinite both ways). Any number of storages can be combined, one argument and one result each, in their order: two stacks already build a Turing-power machine (e.g. aⁿbⁿcⁿ, which is impossible with a pushdown automaton), a queue gives a queue automaton. The automaton operations (det, min…) only apply to storage-free machines — the app explains why.

grammar.heading: Grammar
grammar.example:
Grammar:
  name: G
  charset: a, b
  variables: S
  init: S
  rules:
    - S -> aSb | ε   # type eps for ε; \eps = the letters
grammar.body: The grammar view automatically determines the class according to the Chomsky hierarchy, and for every level shows which rule violates it and why.

grammar.title: Grammar
grammar.epsilonFreeHint: ε occurs at most as S → ε, and S never appears on a right-hand side.
grammar.type3Holds: Every rule has the form A → aB or A → a (S → ε only if S occurs on no right-hand side).
grammar.type2Holds: Every rule has the form A → α with α ≠ ε (S → ε only if S occurs on no right-hand side).
grammar.type1Holds: Every rule has the form βAγ → βαγ with α ≠ ε (S → ε only if S occurs on no right-hand side).
grammar.noDerivableWords: No derivable word found up to length 8.
grammar.moreWordsPossible: …the language may be larger than this (the enumeration covers length 8).
grammar.cykIntro: Row j, column i holds the variables that derive the j letters long subword starting at the i-th letter; the word is derivable when the start symbol is in the top cell.
grammar.cykConverted: The grammar is not in Chomsky normal form, so the table is computed on {{expr}}:
grammar.cykUnambiguous: The word has exactly one derivation tree.
grammar.cykAmbiguous: The word has {{count}} derivation trees — the grammar is ambiguous.
grammar.exact: exact decision with the CYK algorithm

notes.contextFreeForm: Every rule is A → α — only its ε-rules keep it out of type 2: ε-removal (lecture notes 6.3.1) makes it type 2, so its language is context-free (6.14).
notes.rightLinear: Its rules are A → uB, A → u, A → B or A → ε (u a terminal word): not type 3 by the definition, but it turns into a finite automaton, so its language is regular.
notes.leftLinear: Its rules are A → Bu, A → u or A → ε, like the left-regular grammars of lecture notes 4.23: not type 3, but its language is regular.
notes.nonContracting: No rule shortens — a non-contracting grammar (lecture notes 12.5): not of the form βAγ → βαγ, yet its language is context-sensitive (12.6).
